header.title_plain: How oxygen gets from the air to your mitochondria, and why a tenfold range in demand needs a five-fold range in cardiac output
header.evidence_type: Educational chapter, "From the atmosphere to the mitochondrion: the oxygen cascade" (book chapter, University of Ottawa (emeritus)) — a textbook summary of established physiology, not a study. Publication details not printed in the file — year, book title and editors to be added.

confidence.why: Settled science; no claims to test.

practical_relevance.why: Not actionable by itself, but the foundation that makes VO2max, cardiac output, lactate and "aerobic capacity" entries make sense. Good glossary source.

reference.what_it_explains: Oxygen reaches muscle in four steps: breathing moves air into the lungs; oxygen diffuses into blood and binds haemoglobin; the heart pumps blood to the tissues; oxygen diffuses from capillaries into cells and mitochondria. Haemoglobin is the hinge — it carries ~60× more oxygen than blood could dissolve — and its binding curve is shaped so that it loads easily in the lungs and unloads easily in hot, acidic, CO2-rich working muscle. Total oxygen demand varies about tenfold from rest to maximal exercise; the system meets it by raising cardiac output ~5× and oxygen extraction ~2×. Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content. Oxygen content is roughly fixed by haemoglobin; cardiac output is the variable the body adjusts minute to minute.

reference.scope_limits: Nothing about training adaptations, nutrition, or performance; it's a clinical physiology chapter with examples drawn from anaemia, transfusion and heart failure. Mitochondrial oxygen levels in living tissue are, as it notes, still uncertain.

layer2.what_it_means: Three things fall out. First, VO2max is bounded by delivery — mostly cardiac output and haemoglobin — which is why endurance adaptations are about stroke volume, blood volume and capillaries rather than lungs. Second, the right-shift of the haemoglobin curve in hot, acidic muscle is the body helping hard-working tissue; "acidic" is not simply bad. Third, the heart runs near its extraction ceiling at rest, so it depends on blood flow; that is why cardiac disease limits exercise first and why uncontrolled hypertension (higher afterload) matters for anyone training hard.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: Nothing about training adaptations, nutrition, or performance; it's a clinical physiology chapter with examples drawn from anaemia, transfusion and heart failure. Mitochondrial oxygen levels in living tissue are, as it notes, still uncertain.

glossary_candidates.definition: The protein in red blood cells that carries almost all the oxygen in blood.
The S-shaped relationship between oxygen pressure and how much haemoglobin is carrying; its shape lets blood load in the lungs and unload in muscle.
Litres of blood the heart pumps per minute = heart rate × stroke volume.
Blood ejected per heartbeat; the main thing endurance training enlarges.
The fraction of delivered oxygen that tissues actually take; ~25% at rest for the body, ~60% for the heart.
Passive movement of a gas from high to low pressure — how oxygen crosses from air to blood and blood to cell.
Oxygen supply inadequate for demand, at the tissue or cell level.
A compound in red cells that makes haemoglobin release oxygen more readily; rises in anaemia and at altitude.
